svg.title: COBOL to Java: where we stand
svg.text: COBOL to Java: where we stand
129 programs from 6 real mainframe codebases we did not write, translated to Java and checked one evidence step at a time.
'Same output' means equal to GnuCOBOL run under IBM's documented rules; not yet measured on a real IBM mainframe (z/OS). Built from commit c66c6b170 on 2026-11-04.
Our test suite: L5 not yet started
Results: 125 of 129 real programs take every branch; 12 pass the planted-bug test
Each row is one codebase. Left: how far its programs have climbed (an L5 program counts at L4 here). Right: its planted-bug work (L5). Our own test estates sit below, never in a total.
Levels L0-L4: how far each program has climbed
1. Real codebases we did not write: 6 IBM and AWS sample applications, 129 programs
We develop against these, so they are not blind tests; no blind codebase has been measured yet.

svg.text: Every branch is net of 494 reviewed infeasible, 5 undefined by IBM outcomes, each named in its evidence report.
L5 so far: 12,350 of the 18,585 planted bugs run were caught by a test; 5,217 more are explained as harmless
(equivalent or unreachable: reviewed claims, not yet audited).
47% of the 42,693 possible planted bugs have been run.
Separate from these: hand-written ports, not the translator, score 86.8% adjusted and 68.0% raw over 59 ports. They feed no level.
The 4 not at every branch yet, each named: none dropped
All still count in the 129. 3 stop where a ruling stops them; 1 still in progress.
RECORD KEY names a WORKING-STORAGE item; IBM's compiler rejects the source
LE condition handling and SOAP faults that no oracle can back
47 of 48 branch outcomes run (97.9%); L4 needs all
2. Our internal test suites: 85 CICS test programs and 4 Open World practice codebases (pinned v0.7.0)
Written by us to break the translator, never in a total. The CICS programs test one CICS behaviour each.
The practice codebases come before translator support and are not translated yet by design (their first run is measured once, rule 5); the scanner reads 43 of their 44 planted traps correctly.

svg.text: Results by age of code: 1970s to today
Real codebases mix decades: 1980s programs LINK 1990s ones that call 2010s Db2 code. Each program is dated by the features it uses (era_tags.py); 13 show no dating clue.
What the translator can do: 25 mainframe areas, gaps included
7 works, 15 partial, 1 reads only, 1 refused, 1 nothing. Counted from the code on every run; a bar appears only where IBM publishes a full list to count against.
8 tables, 71 rules, 153 test vectors, 162 matrix cells
part of the rules above: depth, not extra rules
US, European, Arabic, Hebrew, Greek, Turkish; Japanese, Chinese, Korean
comma decimal point, pound / euro / rupee signs, lakh grouping, rounding, Lilian dates; 0 failing cells (Cultural Gauntlet)
members as raw exported mainframe bytes
EBCDIC incl. Arabic and Japanese DBCS, Shift-JIS, UTF-8 with and without BOM
FCT, PCT, PPT, DCT, TST, SIT, SRT, JCT, TCT, MCT, PLT, DSNCRCT
12 tables read into the resource map; not run
keyed read, write and browse, in 16 equivalence cases
browse by relative byte address under CICS
0 of 7 rules match IBM; CICS calls only
calls run on our own model, so no rule matches yet
SORT, MERGE, COPY, INCLUDE, OMIT, OUTREC; 4 key formats
REPRO and plain copies; other commands refused
run or bypass per step (COND), CardDemo's 8 COND jobs: 34 of 34 answers
answers written from IBM's JCL Reference before the evaluator ran
143 jobs read in 213 JCL members; 18 depend on COND / IF

How faithful the Java runtime is: 91 of 192 rules match IBM's manuals
Each rule is one documented COBOL or CICS behaviour, judged against IBM's documentation. Measured on z/OS: 0 of 192 so far (#4702).
our choice, written down by name
with a named error, never a guess
